beats.script_body: Look out at the river. It's the reason this great city was built. When Henry Hudson and his crew of sixteen sailed up it in 1609, mistakenly thinking they'd find Asia at its mouth, little did they know they were setting in motion a chain of events that would still be shaping lives over four hundred years later. Hudson's reports about the trading possibilities of the area — particularly for valuable animal pelts — plus his amazement at the great natural harbor here, spurred the Dutch to create settlements. They guessed, rightly, that the harbor of New York would be the linchpin connecting Europe, via the Atlantic, with the interior of this vast and wealthy continent, via the Hudson River. Later, after the building of the Erie Canal, which connected the Hudson with the Great Lakes, New York became the most powerful city in the nation.

physical_cues.cue: Look out at the river and the great natural harbor from the waterfront

key_claims: Henry Hudson sailed up the river in 1609 with a crew of 16, seeking Asia
Hudson's reports on pelts and the harbor spurred Dutch settlement
Erie Canal connected the Hudson with the Great Lakes, making NYC the nation's most powerful city

beats.script_body: This circular stone structure — taller in some earlier incarnations — has been at the center of New York life over the years. In 1807, the West Battery, as it was then called, was built as a fort on a landfill island in the water off Manhattan, to ward off British invasions. It never saw action, however: during the War of 1812 the British attacked Washington, D.C., instead. In 1817 it was renamed Castle Clinton in honor of Mayor De Witt Clinton, and in 1823 the federal government ceded the site to the city.

beats.script_body: In 1855, the space was transformed once more, into the city's first immigrant processing center. Over eight million new arrivals — a full two-thirds of those who came to the United States at this time — spent their first hours in the country here, registering their names with the government, exchanging money, and getting information on jobs, medical care, and lodgings. By 1890, the vast number of immigrants, and the growing problem of outsiders scamming them, necessitated a move to a larger and more easily patrolled offshore space: Ellis Island, which you can see from here, to the right of the Statue of Liberty, its main hall reaching into the sky with four little spires.

beats.script_body: At the base of this flagpole is a bas-relief sculpture depicting the historic scene of Dutch official Peter Minuit 'buying' Manhattan from Native American residents in 1626, to consolidate the Dutch colony in one easily defended spot. Just how the 'sale' went down is still a matter of controversy. Most likely the 'sellers' were the Canarsie tribe who, according to a letter by Dutch merchant Peter Schagen, let the island go for sixty guilders — the equivalent of twenty-four dollars. But did the Indians know they were selling the island, or did they think they were simply accepting shiny trinkets as part of a welcome ceremony? And were the Canarsie even in a position to sell it, as it had long been a communal hunting ground used by a number of tribes? We'll never know the truth, but this is the one place in Manhattan where the most infamous real estate deal in history is memorialized.

beats.poi_name: National Museum of the American Indian
beats.script_body: You are now standing at the foot of Broadway, the thoroughfare that leads all the way to the top of Manhattan, thirteen miles away. The original Dutch fort stood in this exact place. The building in front of you, designed by Cass Gilbert, was one of the most important structures in the city when it was built — the Alexander Hamilton U.S. Customs House. Before 1913, when the federal government instituted the personal income tax, the government's revenue came almost entirely from customs on imported goods. A full seventy-five percent of that revenue came from the Port of New York, processed in this grand Beaux Arts colossus, completed in 1907 and comprising over four hundred and fifty thousand square feet of interior space.

beats.source_passage: You are now standing at the foot of Broadway, the famous thoroughfare that leads all the way to the top of Manhattan, 13 miles away. The original Dutch fort stood in this exact place. But what you see in front of you is a building of just as much significance. Designed by Cass Gilbert, this was one of the most important structures in the city when it was built—the Alexander Hamilton U.S. Customs House. And a full 75% of this revenue came from the Port of New York, where it was processed in this appropriately grand Beaux Arts colossus, completed in 1907 and comprising over 450,000 square feet of interior space.

beats.script_body: It's a wedding cake of an edifice, with dozens of bright white sculptures adorning the gray granite facade. Daniel Chester French was the sculptor — he also did the seated Lincoln at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C. — and his choice of symbols could be read as a treatise on the prejudices of Victorian-era America. The four seated women at the front represent the four 'great' continents. From left to right, they are Asia; the Americas, with South America barely present, tellingly represented by the Aztec-like structure that North America has her foot on; Europe; and Africa. America and Europe look full of vigor and purpose, but Asia has her eyes closed, perhaps in meditation, and Africa — in a metaphor for her supposed lack of vision and power — is in a deep slumber. America shelters a new immigrant crouching to her left, pushing forward a winged wheel, those of the Roman god Mercury, divine overseer of commerce.

beats.source_passage: It's a wedding cake of an edifice, with dozens of bright white sculptures adorning the gray granite facade. Daniel Chester French was the sculptor—he also did the moving sculpture of Lincoln at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C.—and his choice of symbols could be used as a treatise on the prejudices of Victorian-era America. The four women seated at the front represent the four "great" continents of the world. From left to right as you look at them, they are Asia; the Americas (South America, barely present, is tellingly represented by the Aztec-like structure that North America has her foot on); Europe; and Africa. America and Europe look full of vigor and purpose, but Asia has her eyes closed (perhaps in meditation?), and Africa—in a metaphor for her lack of vision and power?—is in a deep slumber. America is sheltering a new immigrant who crouches to her left, and the immigrant is pushing forward a wheel with wings on it, those of the Roman god Mercury, the divine overseer of commerce.

beats.script_body: At the top of the building are twelve more figures, meant to represent the great trading nations of history: Greece, Rome, Phoenicia, Genoa, Venice, Spain, Holland, Portugal, Denmark, England, France, and Belgium. Why Belgium? The official story is that during World War I, 'vandals' carved 'Belgium' across the shield of the figure that had originally been 'Germany.' No explanation has ever been given for how vandals could surreptitiously make such a big change to one of the most visible and heavily guarded buildings in the city.

beats.poi_name: National Museum of the American Indian
beats.script_body: Inside, the rotunda holds WPA murals depicting the great conquistadors — ironic, given the building now houses the National Museum of the American Indian. The staircase on the right as you enter was meant to evoke the inside of a nautilus shell, and in what is now the museum's study center stand the elaborate, imposing rows of teller windows where merchants once paid their customs taxes. Entry to the museum is free, though there is no permanent exhibition.

beats.script_body: On July 9, 1776, the Declaration of Independence was read aloud near City Hall, and a small battalion of agitated colonists marched here to behead the statue of King George that stood in the center of the park. It had been erected just five years earlier by many of these same men, in gratitude for the king's part in repealing the odious Stamp Act — the one that provoked the 'no taxation without representation' movement. Though it can't be proven, legend has it that the lead statue was then melted down and used for cannon balls and bullets in the war against the British. The fence that rings the park is the original, one of the few colonial structures of any sort left in Manhattan; when first erected, its spokes had royal crowns at their tips, and these too were destroyed by the colonists.

beats.script_body: At the uptown end of the park stands Charging Bull. In 1989, a recession inspired artist Arturo Di Modica to create the sculpture as a symbol of bull markets to come. The city hadn't asked for this work of boosterism: Di Modica trucked it over to Wall Street in the dead of night and dumped it below a giant Christmas tree in front of the New York Stock Exchange. The seven-thousand-pound statue proved so popular that the city decided to let the 'gift' stay — though not in its original spot.

beats.script_body: The bad news first: this is not what Fraunces Tavern actually looked like, but a hopeful reconstruction completed in 1904, based on the architectural styles of the period — about forty percent of the building is original. Nonetheless, it was here that the Sons of Liberty met on dozens of occasions to discuss plans for evicting the British. Once the Revolutionary War was over, Fraunces Tavern was the place where George Washington delivered his famous 'Farewell to the Troops,' and where Alexander Hamilton set up his first Office of the Treasury.

beats.script_body: On a more sobering note, in 1975 Fraunces Tavern was bombed by the Armed Forces Puerto Rican National Liberation Front. Four people were killed and dozens injured. The choice of this site had dual reasons: not only is it a symbol of American ideals, it is one of the few important historic buildings in New York with a Caribbean connection — Samuel Fraunces was an immigrant from the West Indies.

beats.script_body: Directly across the street from the tavern is the headquarters of Goldman Sachs, a massive glass-and-brownstone skyscraper that cuts Stone Street in two. When it was being constructed, crews found the foundations of old Governor Lovelace's Tavern, another colonial-era watering hole and briefly the seat of the colonial government. In a compromise with local archaeologists, part of the site was left open with a glass viewing pane atop it. If you walk the perimeter of the skyscraper in the direction you've been going, you can see these excavations through glass panels in the sidewalk — at the end of the rows of benches, one under the colonnade, one in the open air. Take a moment to read the plaques and gaze down.

beats.script_body: Here you'll have a remarkably accurate snapshot of what the city looked like around 1837. This narrow, winding street was the first to be paved in New Amsterdam and the only one thought to still sit where the Dutch colonists originally placed it. All of the buildings went up immediately after the great fire of 1835, which devastated the city, wiping out twenty square blocks. Many blamed the volunteer firefighters of the time who, working in rival squads for cash payment, spent more time fighting one another than the flames — a battle Martin Scorsese's 2002 film Gangs of New York dramatically re-creates.

beats.script_body: Mill Lane has the distinction of being the shortest street on Manhattan — and yes, there was once a mill here. Folk tradition held that it was here that Peter Stuyvesant, the Dutch Director-General of New Amsterdam, signed a treaty of surrender when the British invaded. Thanks to recently uncovered documents, we now know that act actually happened at Stuyvesant's farm, in what is today the East Village. Stuyvesant surrendered unwillingly, having torn to pieces the first letter sent by the British warship commander. City leaders then painstakingly pieced the letter back together; upon seeing its favorable terms — colonists could keep their land and businesses — ninety-three leading citizens, including Stuyvesant's seventeen-year-old son, demanded he surrender the colony. Stuyvesant did so but mourned the loss for the rest of his life.

Folk tradition had it that it was here that Peter Stuyvesant, the Dutch Director-General of New Amsterdam, signed a treaty of surrender when the British invaded. Thanks to recently uncovered documents, we know that historic act actually happened at Stuyvesant's farm, in what is today the East Village. Stuyvesant surrendered unwillingly, having torn to pieces the first letter sent by the British warship commander. City leaders then pieced the letter painstakingly back together. Upon seeing the favorable terms it presented the colonists (they would be allowed to keep their land and businesses), 93 leading citizens—including Stuyvesant's 17-year-old son, a traitorous young fogey—demanded Stuyvesant surrender the colony to the British. Stuyvesant did so but mourned the loss of the colony for the rest of his life.

beats.script_body: If you walk to 74 Wall Street, you'll be standing in the heart of what was once the United States' largest slave market, a bastion of inhumanity that held more auctions than any other in the country. The sale of humans began here in 1711 and was not fully outlawed in New York until 1827, making it one of the last two northern states to do so. There's a small plaque about the market at Water and Wall streets, though most scholars think it was actually here, not there.

beats.script_body: Here is New York's greatest monument to thwarted ambition. Architect H. Craig Severance dreamed of building the tallest building in the world, taller than the Woolworth Building, which had held the record from 1917 to 1930. The trouble was that his former partner and archrival William Van Alen had the same aspiration. In the summer of 1929, at the height of the bubble before Black Tuesday, they began a 'race to the top' — Severance at 40 Wall Street, Van Alen at the Chrysler Building. In a record eleven months, Severance finished this building for the Bank of Manhattan, certain his structure would be the tallest. But Van Alen then administered the coup de grâce he'd hidden in his elevator shaft: the Chrysler Building's iconic Art Deco spire, which added an unbeatable hundred and twenty-five feet. The Chrysler's own title was snatched away just one year later by the Empire State Building.

beats.source_passage: Here is New York's greatest monument to thwarted ambitions. Architect H. Craig Severance had a dream: He wanted to build the tallest building in the world, taller than the Woolworth Building (which held the record from 1917–30). Problem was, his former partner and archrival William Van Alen had the same aspirations, and in the summer of 1929, at the height of the bubble that preceded Black Tuesday (the great stock market crash), they began a "race to the top," Severance at 40 Wall St. and Van Alen at the Chrysler Building (p. 208). In a record 11 months, Severance completed this building for the Bank of Manhattan at 40 Wall St., certain that the Chrysler Building was completed and his structure would be the tallest. But once Severance finished construction, Van Alen administered the coup de grâce that he'd been hiding in the elevator shaft of his building: the Chrysler Building's iconic Art Deco spire, which added an unbeatable 125 feet onto the building. I can only imagine that Severance felt some small measure of satisfaction when the Chrysler's title was snatched from it 1 short year later by the Empire State Building.

Head inside to see the magnificent rotunda, one of the loveliest public spaces in the city; admission is free.

beats.script_body: Note the austere building across the street; it was the headquarters of banker J. P. Morgan — the window of his former office is above the flagpole. Look closely at the side facing Federal Hall and you'll see it is pocked with small indentations: the scars of the Financial District's first terrorist attack, in 1920. One bright, sunny morning, a horse and carriage loaded with explosives parked here. Moments later a huge explosion shook the street, killing thirty-one people and wounding scores more. The blast was so powerful that all that was ever found of the horse was a horseshoe. Police traced it to a blacksmith who vaguely recalled shoeing the horse of an Italian man, and on that scanty evidence the police and press decided the blast must have been the work of Italian anarchists. No one was ever charged.

beats.source_passage: Note the austere, somewhat anonymous-looking building across the street from the hall; it was the headquarters of banker J. P. Morgan (the window of his former office is above the flagpole). If you look closely at the side of the building that faces Federal Hall, you'll notice that it is pocked with small indentations. These are the scars of the Financial District's first terrorist attack, which occurred in 1920. One bright and sunny morning (isn't it odd that these events always seem to occur on beautiful days?), a horse and carriage loaded with explosives parked here. Moments later a huge explosion shook the street, killing 31 people and wounding scores more. The blast was so powerful that all that was ever found of the horse was a horseshoe. The police used this piece of evidence to trace the blacksmith who made it; he had vague recollections of shoeing the horse of an Italian man, and on this scanty piece of evidence the police (and press) decided that the blast must have been the work of Italian anarchists. No one was ever charged with the crime.

beats.script_body: You are now gazing at the most famous — some would say infamous — financial institution in the world. The building's towering columns, crowded ornamental pediment, and huge flag trumpet that this is a place of incomparable might and prestige, far more imposing than the government's plainer Federal Hall across the street. In front of the Exchange is a scraggly buttonwood tree, meant to invoke the buttonwood under which New York's first traders stood in 1792 when they met to begin brokering the Revolutionary War debt — the first stock market in America.

The beautifully fluted, curtainlike limestone of the facade; the spider-web pattern of the cathedral window above the entry; and the sumptuous, soaring lobby remind us of a time when such excess and exquisite workmanship were the norm for places of business — which, in the heady times before the Stock Exchange crash, were conceived as temples of commerce.

beats.script_body: Look down as you amble along Broadway at the brass plates naming the ticker-tape parades held along this stretch. Had you been here in the 1930s or '40s, the crowds would have stood shoulder-to-shoulder, and above your head hundreds at the windows would have showered the street with long paper ribbons of stock quotations spewing from their machines. Read the plates: the catalogue of names is a retread of American history and political alliances. Along with athletes, astronauts, and presidents, you'll find parades for the American hostages released from Iran in 1982, pianist Van Cliburn in 1958, and the controversial President Sukarno of Indonesia in 1956.

beats.source_passage: Look down as you amble along at the brass plates with names and dates listing the ticker-tape parades that have been held along this swatch of Broadway. Had you been here on one of those occasions in the 1930s or '40s, the crowds around you would have been shoulder-to-shoulder, and above your head, hundreds would have been standing at the windows, showering the street with the long paper ribbons of stock market quotations that spewed from their machines, marking the dance of the stock market. Read the plates. The catalogue of names is an interesting retread of American history and political alliances; along with athletes, astronauts, and presidents, you'll find parades for the American hostages released from Iran (1982), pianist Van Cliburn (1958), and the controversial President Sukarno of Indonesia (1956).

_pipeline.discovery_notes: Tier-3 candidate: privately owned park, origin of Occupy Wall Street (Sept 2011). Modern political-history stop.

beats.script_body: There's not much to see anymore, but this private one-block-long park is where the 'Occupy Wall Street' movement started in September of 2011, bringing the concept of the power of the one percent into modern political discourse. Activists occupied the park for almost two months before being forced out on November 15 by the police.
